| [NOTE-590](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-590.md) | The stance triangle | Stance is one act with three aspects: in taking a stance a speaker evaluates an object, thereby positions a subject (usually the self), and thereby aligns with other subjects. The triangle's nodes are two subjects and a shared object; its sides are directed vectors of evaluation (two) and alignment, with positioning reflected back on each subject. Stance belongs to utterances in dialogic context, not to sentences, and needs an object even when none is spoken. A stance follow that resonates with a stance lead must mark the relation (too, either). Argued from Santa Barbara Corpus excerpts; no counts are reported. | Read |

| [NOTE-622](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-622.md) | Making It Explicit | In the core of chapter 3, asserting undertakes a commitment, licenses others to reassert it and takes on a responsibility to show entitlement if challenged. Each interlocutor keeps score of everyone's commitments and entitlements, so scorekeeping is doubly perspectival. | [NOTE-644](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-644.md) | Semantic Unification | Puts basic DRT into sheaf form: a DRS is a section of a presheaf of consistent literals, an anaphoric resolution is a cover by variable maps, and the discourse's meaning is the gluing, unique if it exists (Proposition 1). | [NOTE-710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-710.md) | boyd (2008), Taken Out of Context: collapsed contexts | Networked publics remove the boundaries that kept a person's social contexts apart. Self-presentations that differ by audience coexist while the audiences are segmented, and collide when the medium brings them together. People manage the collision by scripting it (a wedding), by noticing it (meeting the boss while out with friends), or by rebuilding walls (privacy settings, false details). Online, the collision often goes unseen by the person it happens to. | Skimmed |

| [NOTE-736](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-736.md) | Strawson — Intention and Convention in Speech Acts | Austin's thesis that illocutions are conventional fails for warnings, entreaties and objections. Their force is a wholly overt, audience-directed intention: Grice's three intentions plus a fourth, with uptake as the audience's grasp of it. The scheme strains on orders and fails on institutional acts. What all illocutions share is an overt intention meant to be understood. | Read |

| [NOTE-1344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1344.md) | Osmelak et al. — PETra | PETra is a corpus of about 3,000 English-source sentence pairs from TED-Multi and Europarl, in twelve target languages, in which a translation adds or replaces material to make culture-bound knowledge explicit: unit conversions, entity descriptions and specifications, translator glosses. | [NOTE-1432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1432.md) | boyd — Taken Out of Context: networked publics and context collapse | In boyd's full chapters on networked publics, collapsed contexts are one of three dynamics produced by four properties of networked media: without spatial, social and temporal boundaries, distinct contexts are hard to keep apart, and a performer may not see the collision. | [NOTE-1435](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1435.md) | Gutt — Translation and Relevance (thesis, 1989) | Gutt's thesis puts translation under Sperber and Wilson's interpretive use. Utterances resemble each other to the degree that the assumptions each communicates in its own cognitive environment overlap, so identical propositional form does not guarantee identical interpretation. A translation is faithful when it resembles the original closely enough in the respects that make it relevant to its audience, which is a context-dependent standard. Direct translation is complete interpretive resemblance in the context the original envisaged; its communicative clues, from word order to connectives and greetings, are fixed by their effect on interpretation, not by their form. | Skimmed |

| [NOTE-1453](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1453.md) | Harnish — Commitments and Speech Acts | Harnish sets the Gricean expressed-attitude theory against normative theories of illocution. On Bach and Harnish, communicative acts are individuated by the attitude the speaker expresses, that is, reflexively intends the hearer to take the utterance as reason to ascribe. Institutional acts are a separate class. Searle's account of how speech creates commitment is unexplained, and Alston's rule-subjection analysis fails. Expressing the belief that P and taking responsibility for P may be equivalent, so the normative theory may be the same facts redescribed. Teasing and the audience's standing are not discussed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1487](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1487.md) | Wilhoit — Ventriloquism's methodological scope | A short reply to Cooren (2014). Montréal School CCO's commitment to interaction makes conversation analysis its method of choice, so ventriloquism carries epistemological and methodological commitments that other communication traditions will not share, and it cannot be the open metamodel Craig (1999) called for.
